specPoints.text: know that some reactions are reversible and this is indicated by the symbol ⇌ in equations
describe reversible reactions such as the dehydration of hydrated copper(II) sulfate and the effect of heat on ammonium chloride

primer.text: From Rates of Reaction you already know that changing conditions changes how fast reactions run. This note shows that conditions can even change the direction a reaction takes, using the two-arrow symbol that marks a reversible change. Two classic examples, heated ammonium chloride and blue copper sulfate, carry the whole idea.

lessons.title: Reactions that run both ways
lessons.opening: Most equations you have met end when the reactants run out, but some reactions can be undone by their own products. This lesson introduces the double arrow that marks chemistry able to travel in both directions.
keyPoints: In reversible reactions the product molecules can react again or decompose to reform the reactants.
A reversible reaction can occur in both directions at the same time.
The forward reaction forms the products while the reverse reaction forms the reactants.
The symbol with two half arrowheads, one pointing each way, indicates a reversible reaction.
Changing the reaction conditions can change the direction a reversible reaction takes.

low.restatement: Some reactions can be undone: the products can turn back into the reactants, so the change runs both ways. Chemists show this with two arrows, one for each direction of travel.
low.analogy: It is like a two-way street: the same road carries traffic into town and back out, and a diversion can send more cars either way.
low.examPointer: Use the two-way arrow in equations for reversible changes and name the forward and reverse reactions.

medium.restatement: In a reversible reaction the products can react with each other or decompose, reforming the original reactants, so the change proceeds in both directions. The forward reaction builds products, the reverse reaction rebuilds reactants, and the double half-arrow symbol records the two-way traffic.
medium.analogy: A revolving door lets people pass both ways through the same opening; the crowd on each side is the forward and reverse traffic.
medium.examPointer: Draw the two half arrowheads correctly, top to the right and bottom to the left, and label both directions.

check.stem: What distinguishes a reversible reaction from one that goes to completion?

options.text: The products can react or decompose to reform the reactants
options.explanation: Running in both directions is the defining feature of reversibility.

options.text: It happens faster than a completing reaction
options.explanation: Speed is unrelated to reversibility.

options.text: It produces no products at all
options.explanation: Products form; they just can turn back.

options.text: It cannot be written as an equation
options.explanation: Reversible changes have equations with the double arrow.

check.stem: What does each half of the two-arrow symbol represent?

options.text: One half shows the forward reaction and the other the reverse reaction
options.explanation: The two arrowheads record both directions happening at once.

options.text: One shows a fast reaction and one a slow reaction
options.explanation: The arrows carry direction, not speed.

options.text: One shows the reaction is exothermic
options.explanation: Energy direction is not what the symbol encodes.

options.text: Both show the forward reaction twice
options.explanation: The two halves point opposite ways.

check.stem: In the reverse reaction, what is formed?

options.text: The reactants, rebuilt from the products
options.explanation: The reverse direction runs products back to the starting chemicals.

options.text: New products never seen before
options.explanation: The reverse route leads back to the original reactants.

options.text: Only energy
options.explanation: Chemicals, not just energy, are reformed.

options.text: A catalyst
options.explanation: Catalysts are not formed by reactions at all.

check.stem: How can the direction a reversible reaction takes be changed?

options.text: By changing the reaction conditions, such as the temperature
options.explanation: Conditions steer the balance between the two directions.

options.text: By rewriting the equation
options.explanation: Paper changes nothing in the flask.

options.text: The direction is fixed forever
options.explanation: Reversibility means the direction responds to conditions.

options.text: By adding a catalyst to the products only
options.explanation: Catalysts change pace, not direction.

check.stem: Which arrow orientation is correct for the reversibility symbol?

options.text: Two half arrowheads, the top pointing right and the bottom pointing left
options.explanation: That is exactly how the double arrow is drawn.

options.text: Two full arrowheads both pointing right
options.explanation: That is the single forward arrow, not the reversibility symbol.

options.text: One long arrow crossing one short arrow
options.explanation: The symbol is two stacked half arrows.

options.text: Two dots above and below the equation
options.explanation: Dots are not part of the notation.

lessons.title: Two flagship reversible reactions
lessons.opening: Two reactions carry the reversibility flag in exams: a white solid that fizzes apart when heated and re-forms on cooling, and a blue crystal that loses its water and regains it. This lesson writes both equations and their colour stories.
keyPoints: Warm ammonium chloride splits into ammonia and hydrogen chloride gases, which rejoin on cooling.
The reversible equation shows solid ammonium chloride between the two gases with a double arrow.
Hydrated copper(II) sulfate is blue and holds water inside its crystal structure.
Heating drives off the water to leave white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate in an endothermic change.
Adding water to the white powder turns it blue again and gives out a large amount of heat.

low.restatement: Heating ammonium chloride splits it into two gases, and cooling lets the gases rejoin into the white solid. Blue copper sulfate loses its stored water when warmed and turns white, then drinks water back in and turns blue once more.
low.analogy: It is like a sponge: squeeze the water out with effort, and it drinks it back up the moment water is offered.
low.examPointer: Quote the colour changes, blue to white and back, and the direction of each energy change.

medium.restatement: Ammonium chloride decomposes on heating into ammonia and hydrogen chloride, which recombine to the solid as the hot gases cool. Hydrated copper(II) sulfate gives up its stored water on heating to form white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate, and adding water reforms the blue hydrated salt while releasing heat.
medium.analogy: The copper salt is a colour-coded water meter: blue says water is stored, white says the store is empty, and each refill or emptying runs by heat moving one way or the other.
medium.examPointer: Give both equations with the double arrow and attach endothermic to the heating and exothermic to the rehydration.

check.stem: What happens when the hot gases from heated ammonium chloride cool down?

options.text: They recombine to form solid ammonium chloride again
options.explanation: Cooling runs the reverse reaction, rebuilding the white solid.

options.text: They escape as permanent gases
options.explanation: The reverse reaction returns them to the solid.

options.text: They turn into water and nitrogen
options.explanation: No such products appear in this reaction.

options.text: They condense into a liquid
options.explanation: They reform a solid, not a liquid.

check.stem: Why is hydrated copper(II) sulfate blue?

options.text: Because water of crystallisation is held in its structure
options.explanation: The stored water gives the crystals their blue colour.

options.text: Because copper is always blue
options.explanation: The anhydrous form of the same salt is white.

options.text: Because it contains dissolved oxygen
options.explanation: Oxygen is not the colour source here.

options.text: Because it was heated
options.explanation: Heating drives the colour away, not in.

check.stem: What energy change accompanies the dehydration of hydrated copper(II) sulfate?

options.text: Endothermic, because energy is taken in to remove the water
options.explanation: Driving the water out consumes heat.

options.text: Exothermic, because heat is given off while drying
options.explanation: That is the rehydration step.

options.text: No energy change occurs
options.explanation: Removing bound water requires energy.

options.text: The change depends on the colour
options.explanation: Colour records the state, not the energy flow.

check.stem: A few drops of water are added to white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate. What is observed?

options.text: The powder turns blue and the mixture becomes hot
options.explanation: Rehydration reverses the colour and releases heat strongly.

options.text: The powder turns blue and the mixture becomes cold
options.explanation: The reverse reaction is strongly exothermic, not cooling.

options.text: The powder stays white
options.explanation: The colour change is the classic observation.

options.text: The powder fizzes and dissolves
options.explanation: No fizzing occurs in this change.

check.stem: Which equation correctly represents the thermal decomposition of ammonium chloride as reversible?

options.text: NH4Cl (s) between NH3 (g) and HCl (g) with a double arrow
options.explanation: The solid and the two gases face each other across the two-way arrow.

options.text: NH4Cl (s) forming NH3 (g) only, with a single arrow
options.explanation: HCl is missing and the arrow is one-way.

options.text: NH3 (g) plus HCl (g) forming water, with a single arrow
options.explanation: No water forms in this reaction.

options.text: NH4Cl (s) forming N2 (g) and H2 (g), with a double arrow
options.explanation: Those are not the products of this decomposition.

glossary.definition: A reaction whose products can react or decompose to reform the reactants, shown with a double arrow.
The direction of a reversible change that forms the products.
The direction of a reversible change that reforms the reactants.
The removal of water from a substance, as when hydrated copper sulfate is heated.
Water included in the structure of some salts during crystallisation, affecting their shape and colour.
